payload.data: 14 April 1943 (Hawaii date): US Navy codebreakers read JN-25 message NTF131755. Admiral Yamamoto will fly Rabaul to Ballale on 18 April, departing 06:00 Tokyo time (08:00 here) with six fighters. Nimitz authorised the intercept on 17 April. Clock: Henderson Field time, UTC+11; Tokyo time is two hours behind.

Wheels-up 07:25 from Fighter Two (Kukum), Guadalcanal: 18 P-38Gs of the 339th Fighter Squadron, 347th Fighter Group, with pilots from its 12th and 70th Squadrons, on drop tanks. Take-off order and runway heading are reconstructed.
Lt James McLanahan blows a tyre on the take-off roll. Holmes takes his place in Lanphier's attack section.
Lt Joseph Moore's drop tanks will not feed; he turns back and Hine fills the fourth attack slot. Sixteen P-38s continue under radio silence, 10 to 30 ft above the sea.
Mitchell navigates by compass, clock and airspeed alone, 10 to 30 ft above the sea. The track is reconstructed from the published headings, within 20 km.

Lakunai, Rabaul, 06:05–06:10 Tokyo time: Yamamoto boards G4M1 T1-323 (FWO Takeo Kotani); Vice Admiral Ugaki follows in T1-326 (FPO2c Hiroshi Hayashi). Six A6M Zeros of the 204th Kōkūtai escort. The route south-east is a low-confidence reconstruction.
The bombers climb to 6,500 ft; the six Zeros fly 1,500 ft higher at their four o'clock, in two V-formations of three.
08:20, slightly more than 180 miles west of Henderson: Mitchell turns, then flies 27 minutes on 290° and 38 minutes on 305°. The plan kept the track 20 nautical miles off every island (Condon).
Mitchell's plan is to meet the bombers at 09:35, before they reach Ballale. Both formations converge on Bougainville's south-west coast.
Final turn north-east toward the coast, 56 mi out; when it was made is disputed.

Lt Doug Canning breaks radio silence: “Bogeys! Eleven o'clock, high!” (Ames; the report has a quiet “Eleven O' clock”). The Bettys are at 4,500 ft. Tanks drop and Mitchell's twelve climb toward 18,000 ft. Holmes's tanks hang; he and Hine turn out to sea to shake them.

Three Zeros (which section is inferred) peel down in a string at Lanphier; he turns up into them firing and climbs to 6,000 ft. Barber banks hard behind the bombers, which split — T1-323 for the jungle, T1-326 for the sea.
Top cover: Mitchell's twelve climb to 18,000 ft over Empress Augusta Bay, orbiting to meet fighters expected up from Kahili. None come up in time; the cover flight never fires.
Barber fires from directly astern of T1-323 while Zeros make passes on him; its right engine and tail are hit. Inspection of the wreck found only rear-quarter hits.
damaged
destroyed
T1-323 crashes into the jungle inland of Moila Point (6°47.2'S 155°33.1'E). Admiral Yamamoto and all ten others aboard are killed.

Holmes and Hine, back from shedding tanks, drive the Zeros off Barber, then catch T1-326 low over the water off Moila Point; Barber joins and is hit by its debris. Two Zeros chase Lanphier past Kahili at treetop height; he outruns them with two 7.7 mm hits in his tailplane.

T1-326 ditches about 100 m off Moila Point. Ugaki, Hayashi and Captain Kitamura survive; 11 of 14 aboard die.
Past Ballale and Shortland the fighters clash again; Holmes and Barber each claim a Zero. Hine, his left engine smoking, is last seen south of Shortland, losing height on the way home.
damaged
Escort tracks end here. All six Zeros survived: Okazaki landed at Ballale with engine trouble, the rest at Buin; Yanagiya, last down, about 10:20.
Mitchell calls the flight home as Kahili's fighters raise dust taking off; the cover flight never fires. Claimed: three Bettys and three Zeros. Actual Japanese losses: two Bettys, no Zeros.

Holmes, nearly out of fuel, lands in the Russell Islands escorted by Canning; the rest are back on Guadalcanal about 11:40. Japan announces Yamamoto's death on 21 May. Credit for T1-323 remains officially shared between Lanphier and Barber.
